title: Final Exam Summary: Formulae and Nuances
summary: These nine rules cause most of the lost marks in exams. Learn them before the formulas. Count the tails. Two-sided: split $\alpha$ into two parts, $\alpha/2$ in each tail. Use $z_{\alpha/2}$, $t_{\alpha/2}$, $\chi^2_{\alpha/2}$ and $\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}$,…

blocks.x: These nine rules cause most of the lost marks in exams. Learn them before the formulas.
Two-sided: split $\alpha$ into two parts, $\alpha/2$ in each tail. Use $z_{\alpha/2}$, $t_{\alpha/2}$, $\chi^2_{\alpha/2}$ and $\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}$, $f_{\alpha/2}$ and $f_{1-\alpha/2}$.
One-sided: put all of $\alpha$ in one tail. Use $z_\alpha$, $t_\alpha$, $\chi^2_\alpha$ or $\chi^2_{1-\alpha}$, $f_\alpha$ or $f_{1-\alpha}$.
A one-sided bound has one limit only. The other side is open.
A one-sided $95\%$ bound is not the end of a two-sided $95\%$ interval.
The end of a two-sided $95\%$ interval is a one-sided $97.5\%$ bound.
A one-sided $95\%$ bound is the end of a two-sided $90\%$ interval.

Reason. Every $100(1-\alpha)\%$ statement allows a total error of $\alpha$. A two-sided interval can be wrong in two ways ($\mu$ above $U$ or $\mu$ below $L$), so $\alpha$ is shared: $2.5\%$ per side for $95\%$. A one-sided bound can be wrong in one way only, so the whole $5\%$ is used on that side.
Multipliers. $1.960$ belongs to two-sided $95\%$ (each end) and to one-sided $97.5\%$. $1.645$ belongs to two-sided $90\%$ (each end) and to one-sided $95\%$.

Conversion. Each end of a two-sided interval at level $C$ is a one-sided bound at level $C+\tfrac{100-C}{2}$ (for example $95\to97.5$). A one-sided bound at level $C$ is the end of a two-sided interval at level $2C-100$ (for example $95\to90$).

Numerical check (impact-energy data: $\bar{x}=64.46$, standard error $0.316$). Two-sided $95\%$: $(63.84,\,65.08)$. One-sided $95\%$: $\mu\le64.98$ or $\mu\ge63.94$. Two-sided $90\%$: $(63.94,\,64.98)$, which equals the two one-sided $95\%$ bounds. One-sided $97.5\%$ upper bound: $65.08$.
Match each test with the right interval, using the same $\alpha$.
$H_1:\theta>\theta_0$ goes with the lower bound: reject if $\theta_0$ is below it. $H_1:\theta<\theta_0$ goes with the upper bound.

A one-sided test (cutoff $1.645$) can reject while $\theta_0$ is still inside the two-sided $95\%$ interval (cutoff $1.96$). This is not a contradiction. Compare a one-sided test with a one-sided bound, or with the two-sided $90\%$ interval.
Put the claim you want to prove in $H_1$. Rejecting $H_0$ is a strong conclusion. Failing to reject only means there is not enough evidence. It never proves $H_0$.
Read the $P$-value correctly. $P$ is the probability of a result at least this extreme if $H_0$ is true. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true. Reject $H_0$ when $P\le\alpha$.
Read confidence correctly. The $95\%$ describes the method: $95\%$ of intervals made this way contain the parameter. It does not give a probability for one computed interval.

Know the three intervals. A confidence interval bounds a parameter. A prediction interval bounds one future value and is always wider. A tolerance interval bounds a stated proportion of the population.
State and check the assumptions. Normal population for $t$, $\chi^2$ and $F$. Independent samples. Equal variances for the pooled $t$-test and for ANOVA.
Use the eight steps for every test. Parameter; $H_0$; $H_1$; $\alpha$; test statistic; rejection rule; computation; conclusion in words.
Full tables for $z$, $t$, $\chi^2$ and $F$, with one-tail and two-tail columns, are in Chapter 16.
Method of moments: equate $\Exp[X^k]$ to $\frac1n\sum X_i^k$ and solve
Maximum likelihood: maximise $\prod f(x_i;\theta)$, usually through $\ln L$: $\text{Bernoulli: }\hat{p}=\bar{x}$
Exact for normal populations; approximate by the CLT when $n\ge30$.
$\bar{X}$, $S^2$ (divisor $n-1$) and $\hat{P}=X/n$ are unbiased, but $S$ is biased for $\sigma$ ($\Exp[S]=c_4\sigma$; $c_4=0.94,\ 0.9727,\ 0.9896$ for $n=5,10,25$).
A biased estimator can have a smaller MSE than an unbiased one. $\bar{X}$ is the MVUE of $\mu$ for a normal sample.
MLE invariance: the MLE of $h(\theta)$ is $h(\hat\theta)$, so the MLE of $\sigma$ is $\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2}$, not $s$. The normal $\hat\sigma^2$ has divisor $n$: biased, but asymptotically unbiased.
Uniform$(0,a)$: the likelihood has no stationary point, so calculus fails and $\hat{a}=\max x_i$.

Bayes: posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\times$ prior; Bernoulli with a $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ prior gives $\mathrm{Beta}(a+x,\,b+n-x)$. Bootstrap: resample with replacement; the spread of $\hat\theta^*$ estimates $\se(\hat\theta)$.

Conclusion. The estimated failure rate is $0.0462$ per hour.

Conclusion. Estimator 2 is better in the MSE sense even though it is biased.
Conclusion. There is about a $0.6\%$ chance that the sample mean is below $95$.
Conclusion. The new process beats the old by at least $25$ hours with probability $0.984$.

The $\sigma^2$ interval is not symmetric and is very sensitive to non-normality. The proportion interval needs $np\ge5$ and $n(1-p)\ge5$.

sections.title: Chapter 9: Tests on a Single Sample (book Chapter 3)

blocks.x: Compute the test statistic ($z_0$, $t_0$, $\chi_0^2$ or $f_0$). Find the critical value in the table. Then look at the sign in $H_1$: it tells you which tail to check.
$H_1$ has $\ne$ (two-sided): reject if the statistic is far from zero in either direction. For $z$ and $t$, reject if $\abs{\text{statistic}}>$ critical value at $\alpha/2$.
$H_1$ has $>$ (one-sided, right tail): reject if the statistic is larger than the critical value at $\alpha$.
$H_1$ has $<$ (one-sided, left tail): reject if the statistic is smaller than minus the critical value at $\alpha$. (For $\chi^2$ and $F$, smaller than the lower-tail point.)
If the statistic does not pass the critical value, do not reject $H_0$.
$P$-value form of the same rule: reject if $P\le\alpha$.

Example: $z_0=2.4$. One-sided $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ at $\alpha=0.05$: $z_\alpha=1.645$ and $2.4>1.645$, so reject. Two-sided at $\alpha=0.05$: $z_{\alpha/2}=1.96$ and $\abs{2.4}>1.96$, so reject. If $z_0=-2.4$ with $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$, the statistic is on the wrong side, so do not reject.
Each tail holds $\alpha/2$, so look up the table at one-tail area $\alpha/2$.

Statistical significance is not practical significance: with a huge $n$, a trivial shift gives a tiny $P$.

blocks.x: Means, upper bound (here $\sigma_D=\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}$; with unknown $\sigma$ use $t_{\alpha,\cdot}$ and $s$): $\mu_1-\mu_2\le(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)+z_\alpha\,\sigma_D$

Pooled versus Welch: with $n_1=n_2$ they coincide. Pooled misleads when variances differ and $n_1\ne n_2$. Decide from the normal plots, not a preliminary $F$-test; very different slopes mean use Welch.
Paired: $\Var(\bar{D})=2\sigma^2(1-\rho)/n$. Pairing helps when units are heterogeneous and $\rho$ is large; it costs $n-1$ degrees of freedom. Never run an independent test on paired data.
The $F$-test is not robust to non-normality; its two-sided $P$-value adds the tails of $f_0$ and $1/f_0$.
For $n_1,n_2>40$ use $s_i$ in the $z$-test. Test the proportion difference with the pooled $\hat{p}$ but build the interval with the unpooled standard error.
Cause and effect needs randomisation; observational differences can be confounded (Simpson’s paradox).
Given. Method A: $n_1=10$, $\bar{x}_1=48.2$, $s_1=3.1$. Method B: $n_2=12$, $\bar{x}_2=45.1$, $s_2=3.7$. $H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2$ against $H_1:\mu_1\ne\mu_2$, $\alpha=0.05$, equal variances.
Conclusion. The means differ (barely). The interval agrees with the test.
Given. Same samples, but do not assume equal variances. $a_1=s_1^2/n_1=0.961$, $a_2=s_2^2/n_2=1.141$.
Conclusion. Same conclusion as the pooled test.
Conclusion. The mean difference is not zero.
Conclusion. No evidence that the variances differ.
Conclusion. No evidence of a difference. The test uses the pooled $\hat{p}$; the interval uses the unpooled standard error.

sections.title: Chapter 11: Simple Linear Regression and Correlation (book Chapter 5)

blocks.x: Test of $\rho=0$ ($n-2$ df; same as the slope test)
$\hat\sigma^2$ divides by $n-2$ (two parameters estimated). $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)=-\bar{x}\sigma^2/S_{xx}$. The $\hat\beta$’s are unbiased and BLUE.
The $t$-test allows one-sided alternatives; the $F$-test does not. One-sided bounds use $t_{\alpha,n-2}$.
Both intervals are narrowest at $x_0=\bar{x}$; the prediction interval is always wider. The confidence level applies to one $x_0$, not the whole line.
$R^2$ does not measure the slope or whether the model is correct, and it always rises with more terms.

Residuals: standardised $d_i=e_i/\hat\sigma$ (about $95\%$ within $\pm2$). A curve means the wrong form; a funnel means transform $y$ ($\sqrt{y}$, $\ln y$, $1/y$). Linearise $y=\beta_0e^{\beta_1x}$ by $\ln y$, $y=\beta_0x^{\beta_1}$ by logs of both.
Correlation is not causation, and $\rho=0$ is not independence. Textbook values: oxygen purity $\hat\beta_1=14.947$, $\hat\beta_0=74.283$, $R^2=0.877$.
Conclusion. The slope is highly significant, and $99.7\%$ of the variability is explained.
Given. Continue from the fitted line. $\hat{y}_0=0.05+1.99(3.5)=7.015$. Use $t_{0.025,3}=3.182$.
Conclusion. The prediction interval is wider because it includes the variation of a single new observation.
High leverage: $h_{ii}>2p/n$. Influential: $D_i>1$. Beware hidden extrapolation.

Model building: all possible regressions (minimum $MS_E$, $C_p\approx p$, using the full-model $MS_E$); stepwise uses $f_{\mathrm{in}}\ge f_{\mathrm{out}}$ (default $\alpha=0.15$); forward only adds, backward only removes. Selection makes the reported $P$-values optimistic.

Multicollinearity: $\mathrm{VIF}>10$ is a concern (some use $4$–$5$). Sign: significant overall $F$ but insignificant individual $t$’s. Fixes: more data, drop terms, ridge $(X\T X+\lambda I)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y}$. Interpolation can stay accurate; extrapolation cannot.
Given. Remove one regressor. The reduced model has $SS_R=400$, so $SS_R(\beta_j\mid\text{others})=420-400=20$. Use $MS_E=5$ from the full model.
Conclusion. This regressor is not significant. Dropping it is reasonable.
Conclusion. This observation has high leverage. Check Cook’s distance ($D_i>1$ means influential).
$F$ is upper-tail only because $\Exp[MS_{\text{Tr}}]=\sigma^2+n\sum\tau_i^2/(a-1)$. A balanced design is robust to unequal variances.
LSD is liberal (experimentwise error exceeds $\alpha$); Tukey keeps the overall error at $\alpha$. Both are two-sided.
Residual checks: normal plot, residuals versus fitted ($\ln y$ or $\sqrt{y}$ if the variance grows with the mean), and versus run order.
In a random-effects model test $\sigma_\tau^2$, not individual $\tau_i$.
RCBD: blocking costs $b-1$ degrees of freedom; when in doubt, block. The $F$ for blocks is not a reliable test.
Sample size: $\Phi^2=n\sum\tau_i^2/(a\sigma^2)$ with OC curves; textbook $a=5$, $\sum\tau_i^2=5\sigma^2$, power $0.90$ gives $n=6$.
Conclusion. The three settings do not all have the same mean.
Given. Continue from the ANOVA above: $MS_E=1.667$, $n=4$, $9$ error df.
Conclusion. Setting B differs from both A and C; A and C cannot be separated.
Degrees of freedom: $A:\ a-1,\quad B:\ b-1,\quad AB:\ (a-1)(b-1),\quad E:\ ab(n-1),\quad T:\ abn-1$
Each effect is tested with $F=MS/MS_E$; test the interaction $AB$ first.
Effect, sum of squares, coefficient ($C$ = contrast from the sign table)
Curvature test with centre points ($1,\ n_C-1$ df)

Main effect (two levels) is the average at high minus the average at low. The interaction $AB$ is the difference of the diagonal averages. A significant interaction means read the cell means, not the main effects.
One observation per cell: assume no interaction and use $MS_{AB}$ as error. Three factors need $n\ge2$. With $A$ fixed and $B$ random, test $A$ against $MS_{AB}$ and $B$ against $MS_E$.
Single replicate: normal plot of the effects, or pool high-order interactions as error. Dropping $h$ factors projects onto a $2^{k-h}$ with $n2^h$ replicates.
Blocking: $L=\sum\alpha_ix_i\pmod2$; confound the highest-order interaction ($2^3$ with $ABC$: blocks $\{(1),ab,ac,bc\}$ and $\{a,b,c,abc\}$). $2^p$ blocks lose $2^p-1$ effects.

Fractions $2^{k-p}$: aliases come from multiplying by the defining relation ($A^2=I$); each effect has $2^p-1$ aliases; resolution is the length of the shortest word. III: main effects aliased with two-factor interactions; IV: main effects clear, two-factor interactions aliased in groups; V: both clear.

Examples: $2^{3-1}_{\mathrm{III}}$ ($I=ABC$), $2^{4-1}_{\mathrm{IV}}$ ($I=ABCD$), $2^{6-2}_{\mathrm{IV}}$ ($I=ABCE=BCDF=ADEF$), $2^{7-4}_{\mathrm{III}}$ saturated. The alternate fraction $I=-ABC$ de-aliases.
Response surfaces: steepest ascent far from the optimum; central composite design and canonical analysis near it.
Conclusion. The effect of $A$ is large and positive, $B$ is negative, and the interaction is small.
Multiply by $ABC$. Use $A^2=B^2=C^2=I$: $A\cdot ABC=BC$, so $A=BC$; likewise $B=AC$ and $C=AB$.
Resolution. The shortest word in $I=ABC$ has $3$ letters, so the design has resolution III.
Conclusion. Each main effect is aliased with a two-factor interaction.
Sign test: drop ties. One-sided puts all of $\alpha$ in one tail, so use the table column for two-sided $2\alpha$; for $H_1:\tilde\mu>\tilde\mu_0$ reject when $r^-$ is small.

Signed-rank (symmetric continuous population): rank $\abs{x_i-\mu_0}$ with average ranks for ties. One-sided: $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ rejects if $w^-\le w^*$; $H_1:\mu<\mu_0$ rejects if $w^+\le w^*$. Normal approximation for $n\ge20$.
Rank-sum (Mann–Whitney): $W_1$ is the rank sum of the smaller sample; reject if $w_1$ or $w_2\le w_\alpha$. Normal approximation for $n_1,n_2>8$.
Efficiency versus the $t$-test: about $0.95$ for the Wilcoxon tests with normal data and never below $0.86$; the sign test is about $2/\pi\approx0.64$.
Kruskal–Wallis: use the tie-corrected form with many ties. If ANOVA on ranks disagrees with ANOVA on the raw data, trust the ranks.
Textbook values: sign test $n=20$, $r^+=14$, $P=0.1153$; signed-rank $w=60$ against $w^*=52$.
Given. $H_0:\tilde\mu=\tilde\mu_0$ against $H_1:\tilde\mu\ne\tilde\mu_0$. Of $n=12$ nonzero differences, $9$ are positive. Under $H_0$, $R^+\sim\mathrm{Bin}(12,\tfrac12)$.
Table check. $\min(9,3)=3$ and $r^*_{0.05}=2$ for $n=12$; $3>2$, so again do not reject.
Conclusion. No evidence that the median differs from $\tilde\mu_0$.
Conclusion. The mean difference is not zero.
Conclusion. No evidence that the means differ.
Design: $K=\tfrac12\sigma$ and $H=4\sigma$ or $5\sigma$; a $1\sigma$ shift is detected in $8.38$ or $10.4$ samples.
A control chart is a repeated hypothesis test. Never plot specification limits on it.

Western Electric rules: (1) a point beyond $3\sigma$; (2) two of three beyond $2\sigma$ on one side; (3) four of five beyond $1\sigma$ on one side; (4) eight in a row on one side. Do not add them to a CUSUM.
Build limits from $20$–$25$ preliminary samples of size $4$–$6$; remove samples with assignable causes and recompute; check the $R$ chart first.

$\mathrm{PCR}=1$ means $0.27\%$ ($2700$ ppm) fallout; minimum $1.33$, critical $1.66$, six-sigma $2.0$ ($3.4$ ppm with a $1.5\sigma$ shift). $\mathrm{PCR}=\mathrm{PCR}_k$ iff centred. Capability is meaningful only for a stable process.
A $1\sigma$ shift with $n=1$ takes $43.9$ points on average to detect. Narrower limits raise false alarms.
Other tools: histogram, Pareto chart, fishbone diagram, defect-concentration diagram, scatter diagram, check sheet.
Conclusion. Plot each sample mean and range against these limits.
Given. Average fraction defective $\bar{p}=0.40$ ($800$ defectives in $2000$ units); subgroup size $n=100$.
Conclusion. The process is capable but off-centre, because $\mathrm{PCR}_k<\mathrm{PCR}$.
After a shift. If each sample signals with probability $p=0.50$, then $\mathrm{ARL}=1/0.50=2$ samples.
Conclusion. A larger sample size or more frequent sampling shortens the detection time.
Given. Target $\mu_0=99$, $K=1$, $H=10$. Observations $x=100,\ 102,\ 101,\ 103$. Upper sum: $S_H(i)=\max[0,\ x_i-(\mu_0+K)+S_H(i-1)]$, start at $0$.
Conclusion. All values are below $H=10$, so there is no signal yet, but the sum keeps rising, which suggests an upward drift.

sections.title: Which procedure? A quick decision guide

blocks.x: One mean? $\sigma$ known (or $n\ge40$): $z$. $\sigma$ unknown, normal: $t$. Not normal and small: sign or signed-rank.
Two means, independent? Known $\sigma$: $z$. Unknown equal: pooled $t$. Unknown unequal (or in doubt): Welch. Not normal: rank-sum.
Two means, matched pairs? Paired $t$ on the differences (or sign / signed-rank).
Two variances? $F$ (not robust). Two proportions? Pooled $z$ for the test, unpooled for the interval.
More than two means? One factor: ANOVA $F$, then LSD or Tukey; non-normal: Kruskal–Wallis. With a nuisance factor: RCBD. Several factors: factorial ANOVA, $2^k$, fractions.
Relationship? One regressor: simple regression, $t$ or $F$ for $\beta_1$; several: multiple regression with partial $F$; both variables random: correlation.
Distribution fit or independence of categories? $\chi^2$ goodness of fit or contingency table.
Monitoring a process? Mean and spread: $\bar{X}$–$R$ or $\bar{X}$–$S$; individuals; attributes: $P$, $U$; small shifts: CUSUM.
Count tails first: $\alpha/2$ for two-sided, $\alpha$ for one-sided, and one limit only for a bound.
State the model assumptions and check them (normal plot, residuals, equal variances).

Degrees of freedom: $n-1$ ($t$, $\chi^2$, paired), $n_1+n_2-2$ (pooled), $n-2$ (simple regression), $n-p$ (multiple), $N-a$ (one-way), $ab(n-1)$ (two-way), $(a-1)(b-1)$ (RCBD error), $k-p-1$ (goodness of fit).
Round sample sizes up; keep the strong claim in $H_1$; report an interval with every test.
